**问题**：新 abstract 将原来的 "trading approximately 3× more total evaluations for 3× fewer items" 改为 "at the cost of 2.9× more evaluations per item"。

**数学验证**：
- 2.9× 作为 **total evaluations** 比率：1,602 / 552 = 2.9× ✓（这是原文的含义）

**建议修改方向**：
- 改回 "2.9× more total evaluations"
- 或 "at the cost of approximately 3× more evaluations overall"
- 或 "requiring 9 evaluations per item instead of 1"

其余修订均合理：去掉了具体数字（"eight"、"7-9B"、"2.3M"），更紧凑，~143 words（<200 ✓）。

toolUseResult.originalFile: Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation results vary across reproductions, but variance sources interact, and their relative importance shifts with the benchmark format. We apply Generalizability theory (G-theory) in a fully crossed design with up to seven facets across open-weight instruction-tuned models and five benchmarks. Under binary correctness scoring, a recommended 3-prompt $\times$ 3-seed design achieves $G \geq 0.80$ with 178 items---a 3.1$\times$ item reduction over single-condition designs at the cost of 2.9$\times$ more evaluations per item---a tradeoff that favors multi-facet designs when item construction is costly. Variance decomposition reveals that models differ primarily in which items they find difficult rather than in overall ability, and that the variance structure shifts qualitatively between multiple-choice and free-form benchmarks. Preliminary validation across model scales and architecture families confirms structural stability. We release an open-source G-theory pipeline and D-study budget calculator for evaluation design optimization.

We apply Generalizability theory (G-theory) in a fully crossed design with up to seven facets across open-weight instruction-tuned models and five benchmarks. Under binary correctness scoring, a recommended 3-prompt $\times$ 3-seed design achieves $G \geq 0.80$ with 178 items---a 3.1$\times$ item reduction over single-condition designs at the cost of 2.9$\times$ more total evaluations---a tradeoff that favors multi-facet designs when item construction is costly. Variance decomposition reveals that models differ primarily in which items they find difficult rather than in overall ability, and that the variance structure shifts qualitatively between multiple-choice and free-form benchmarks. Preliminary validation across model scales and architecture families confirms structural stability. We release an open-source G-theory pipeline and D-study budget calculator for evaluation design optimization.

lines: Existing studies examine individual variance sources in isolation. \citet{sclar2024formatting} and BrittleBench \citep{brittlebench2026} documented 50--76\% accuracy swings from prompt formatting; \citet{yuan2025layercast} showed up to 9\% variation from numerical precision; \citet{pezeshkpour2024ordering}, \citet{dodge2020finetuning}, and \citet{henderson2018deep} documented ordering and hyperparameter sensitivity---each holding other factors fixed. \citet{messing2026hidden} applied G-theory to LLM evaluation across five methodology facets on a single benchmark (judge identity: 43.8\%), but excluded infrastructure facets and cross-benchmark comparison. \citet{madaan2024quantifying} proposed per-factor metrics without crossing factors. IRT approaches \citep{polo2024tinybenchmarks, lalor2019irt, zhou2026irt} optimize item selection but ignore prompt, seed, and ordering facets. \citet{bouthillier2021accounting} established ANOVA-based variance decomposition for ML reproducibility. Three gaps remain: no study has (a) crossed infrastructure and methodology facets in a unified factorial design, (b) compared variance structures across response formats, or (c) translated variance components into design-dependent reproducibility budgets.

-We address these gaps with a multi-benchmark G-theory study \citep{shavelson1991generalizability, brennan2001generalizability} crossing up to seven facets across eight open-weight 7--9B parameter models and five benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, GSM8K, MATH), totaling approximately 2.3 million records. D-study projections show that a recommended 3-prompt $\times$ 3-seed design achieves $G \geq 0.80$ with 178 items (1,602 evaluations per model), a 3.1$\times$ reduction from 552 single-condition items; the full 1,296-condition design further reduces to 55 items as a theoretical ceiling (Figure~\ref{fig:teaser}). Model$\times$item interaction (up to 36\%) indicates that models differ primarily in \emph{which items} they find difficult \citep{pezeshkpour2024ordering, polo2024tinybenchmarks}.
